target_output:
The key difference between **Google Stadia** (a cloud gaming service, now discontinued) and **YouTube video** is that they handle video in fundamentally different ways, even if both display 1080p resolution. Stadia’s 1080p stream can use **5–10 times more data** than a typical 1080p YouTube video. Here’s why:

---

### 1. Real-time encoding vs. pre-encoded file
- **YouTube:** Videos are pre-compressed using highly efficient, offline encoders (e.g., VP9, AV1) that can spend hours analyzing each frame to squeeze every bit of compression. The stream can also buffer seconds or even minutes of video ahead – the player can download data in advance without you noticing.
- **Stadia:** The game is rendered and encoded *in real-time*. The encoder has only a few milliseconds to compress each frame, so it cannot use the most complex compression techniques. This results in a much higher bitrate to maintain acceptable image quality.

### 2. Latency vs. buffering
- **YouTube:** A 1080p video stream can afford to buffer several seconds of content. The video player can request data in bursts and even let the buffer run low without you seeing stuttering. This allows the encoder to smooth out bitrate spikes and lean on buffering to hide network hiccups.
- **Stadia:** Because it’s an interactive game, you cannot “buffer ahead.” The next frame literally depends on your controller input. Any extra delay (latency) would make the game feel sluggish. Stadia therefore sends a constant, steady stream of data at a higher bitrate to ensure that each frame arrives as quickly as possible, with zero buffering. That uses more total data.

### 3. Frame rate
- **YouTube:** A lot of 1080p content is still 30 fps (frames per second). Even 60 fps uploads are less common and often use a higher bitrate tier, but typical “1080p” video often runs at 30 fps.
- **Stadia:** The **default performance target** was 1080p at **60 fps** (and sometimes 120 fps). Doubling the frame rate roughly doubles the amount of data per second if the compression efficiency is similar. Even if a YouTube video is 60 fps, the real-time encoding penalty still pushes Stadia’s bitrate far higher.

### 4. Quality requirements during motion
- **YouTube:** Viewers tolerate some compression artifacts (blockiness) during fast motion, especially on lower bitrates. The pre-encoded video can allocate bits intelligently across scenes.
- **Stadia:** Compression artifacts directly hurt gameplay – subtle blurring can hide detail needed to spot an enemy, and blocky compression can make UI text unreadable. To keep the image crisp in every fast-moving frame, the encoder must use a **much higher constant bitrate**, often around 15–25 Mbps for 1080p 60 fps.

### Typical data usage comparison
| Service | 1080p Bitrate (approx.) | Data per hour (approx.) |
|---------|-------------------------|--------------------------|
| YouTube (30 fps) | 2–4 Mbps | 0.9–1.8 GB |
| YouTube (60 fps) | 4–8 Mbps | 1.8–3.6 GB |
| Google Stadia (60 fps) | 12–20 Mbps | 5.4–9 GB |

These numbers can vary, but Stadia easily used 2–4× the data of a YouTube 60 fps stream and up to 10× of a 30 fps one.

---

**In short:** Stadia must encode and transmit every frame instantly, without buffering, at a high frame rate, with enough quality to be playable – all of which forces a much higher data rate than a pre-compressed, buffered video stream like YouTube.

The misunderstanding is this: **Data usage isn’t determined by resolution alone; it’s determined by bitrate**, which is the number of *bits* (data) used per second to describe those pixels. Two streams can both be exactly 1920×1080, but one might use 2 megabits per second (Mbps) and another 20 Mbps – that’s a 10× difference in data usage per hour, yet both are “1080p”.

So the “bitrate stuff” is not a separate issue – **it is *the* issue**. It’s the direct measure of how much data the service sends you. When you ask “why does Stadia use more data?”, you’re really asking “why is Stadia’s bitrate so much higher for the same resolution?” And that comes down to the real-time encoding constraints I mentioned earlier.

Think of it like two copies of the same 1000-page book:
- **YouTube** is like a tiny mass-market paperback – the printer spent hours pre-compressing the text, using thin paper and a small font. The book still has all the words (all the pixels), but it’s light and uses very little material (data).
- **Stadia** is like someone writing out that exact same book by hand, in thick marker, on thick cardstock, one page every 1/60th of a second, with no time to plan. The pages are still 1000, but the amount of paper (data) is far, far higher because the process can’t be made as efficient.

In video terms, YouTube’s pre-encoded, buffered stream can describe each 1080p frame with very few bits because it’s been heavily compressed offline. Stadia’s live game feed can’t use those highly efficient techniques, so it needs many more bits per frame to avoid turning the image into a blocky mess – and those extra bits *are* the extra data.

**So, to sum up:**  
Same pixel count → same “picture” in terms of resolution.  
Different bitrates → different amounts of data to transmit those pixels every second.  
Stadia’s data usage is higher because its real-time, zero-buffering pipeline forces a much higher bitrate for the same 1080p resolution. There’s no contradiction – it’s exactly why the bitrate (and thus the data) differs.
